Chapter Two: The Weight of Words and the Power of Silence.
You know, language really is a powerful thing. It’s a tool we all use every day, but sometimes, it turns into a weapon without us even realizing it. Think about it—how often do words just slip out, maybe in the middle of a chat with a coworker or during a quick conversation with a neighbor? Sometimes those words are meant to be harmless, but their impact can run deep. Picture a colleague tossing out a comment about “articulate” speech, totally unaware of what that might imply. Or maybe a neighbor cracks a joke about someone’s hair, not knowing the history or the pain tied to that topic. Those words stick with you. They echo in your head long after the conversation’s over. And if you’re on the receiving end, there’s this constant calculation going on in your mind. Should you say something? Will it even matter if you do? Most of the time, it just feels easier to let it go. The idea of having to explain or educate someone—it’s exhausting. So, you end up carrying those words, adding them to a growing pile of small hurts and misunderstandings. But here’s something to pay attention to—silence isn’t always a choice. Sometimes, it’s what you need to keep yourself safe. Imagine a student in class, listening as a teacher mispronounces their name. They want to correct them, but they stay quiet. Or think about an employee at work, laughing along with a joke that actually stings, just so they’re not labeled as “too sensitive.” That kind of silence is heavy. It protects you, but it can also weigh you down. Every now and then, though, that silence breaks. Maybe a friend finally decides to speak up, naming the hurt that’s been building up inside. Yeah, the conversation feels awkward—maybe even painful—but it’s also important. In those moments, there’s this huge sense of relief. Sure, the words might not come out perfectly, but at least they’re honest. And it’s not all negative. Sometimes, language is what brings us together. Sharing stories in private, whispering the things that are hard to say out loud—that’s how we start to heal. There’s this quiet understanding in those conversations, a kind of gentle reminder that, yes, the pain is real, but you’re not alone in it. Still, we can't ignore that language cuts both ways. It can open up, but it can also hide things away. In public, people often steer clear of talking about race. It’s too uncomfortable, too likely to cause a stir. But that kind of silence? It’s deafening. It’s like refusing to see the truth that so many people live with every single day.
